context: Maximally structured causal metadata: labels, levels, role, category, description, causal mechanism, direct parents, direct children, Markov blanket members, CPT shape hints (which parent state combinations most strongly drive each level), and quantitative actuarial notes where available. Designed to provide the richest possible prior for causal graph recovery in the Insurance network.

variables.name: GoodStudent
variables.label: Good student status
variables.description: Whether the driver qualifies as a good student (GPA ≥ 3.0 or equivalent).
variables.mechanism: GoodStudent is a binary indicator jointly determined by Age (primarily Adolescent/young Adult) and SocioEcon (academic performance correlates with socioeconomic resources and parental investment). It serves as a risk proxy that feeds RiskAversion: good students are empirically more likely to be Cautious or Normal drivers. Not a vehicle or cost node.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(GoodStudent=True) highest when Age=Adolescent and SocioEcon=UpperMiddle or Wealthy (~0.40); lowest when Age=Senior (~0.01). SocioEcon=Prole + Age=Adolescent → P(True) ≈ 0.20.
variables.quantitative_notes: Insurance industry: good-student discount typically 5–15% premium reduction. In the Insurance BN, GoodStudent is one of three nodes feeding RiskAversion (along with no other direct parents of RiskAversion), making it an important confound between demographic profile and behavioural risk.

variables.name: Age
variables.label: Driver age group
variables.description: Driver's age bracket; the most broadly connected demographic root node.
variables.mechanism: Root node with no modeled parents. Age has three direct downstream effects: GoodStudent (Adolescent most eligible), SeniorTrain (Senior-only intervention), and DrivingSkill (Adolescent and Senior both have elevated SubStandard probability due to inexperience and age-related decline respectively). Age is the most connected root node in the driver sub-network.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(DrivingSkill=SubStandard | Age=Adolescent) ≈ 0.50; P(DrivingSkill=SubStandard | Age=Adult) ≈ 0.10; P(DrivingSkill=SubStandard | Age=Senior) ≈ 0.35. P(SeniorTrain=True) > 0 only for Age=Senior.
variables.quantitative_notes: IIHS data: drivers aged 16–19 have crash rates 3× higher than adults 20–59. Drivers aged 70+ have elevated rates primarily due to fragility and slower reaction time. The Age=Senior + SeniorTrain interaction is the key intervention pathway in the model: completed training can raise P(DrivingSkill=Normal) from ~0.45 to ~0.65 for Senior drivers.

variables.name: SocioEcon
variables.label: Socio-economic status
variables.description: Household socio-economic tier; shapes vehicle and neighbourhood choices.
variables.mechanism: Root node with no modeled parents. SocioEcon is the primary economic constraint variable: it determines vehicle tier (MakeModel), residential location (HomeBase), and contributes to GoodStudent. Wealthy drivers drive Luxury/SuperLuxury vehicles in Secure/Suburb areas; Prole drivers drive Economy vehicles in City/Rural areas. SocioEcon is the root that connects vehicle quality to neighbourhood theft risk.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(MakeModel=Luxury or SuperLuxury | SocioEcon=Wealthy) ≈ 0.65; P(MakeModel=Economy | SocioEcon=Prole) ≈ 0.60. P(HomeBase=Secure | SocioEcon=Wealthy) ≈ 0.55; P(HomeBase=City | SocioEcon=Prole) ≈ 0.50.
variables.quantitative_notes: Socio-economic status is the dominant upstream variable in the Insurance network's vehicle sub-tree. Its indirect effect on theft (via HomeBase and CarValue) and on safety features (via MakeModel → Antilock, Airbag) means SocioEcon is a common cause confound between multiple seemingly unrelated outcomes.

variables.name: RiskAversion
variables.label: Risk aversion tendency
variables.description: Dispositional risk attitude; primary behavioural input to driving quality.
variables.mechanism: RiskAversion is influenced by GoodStudent (good students trend Cautious). It is the behavioural component of DrivQuality (interacting with DrivingSkill) and also drives Mileage exposure (risk-seeking drivers drive more). It is the key node bridging demographic background and accident risk: high risk aversion can partly compensate for low driving skill, and vice versa.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(RiskAversion=Cautious | GoodStudent=True) ≈ 0.35; P(RiskAversion=Psychopath | GoodStudent=False) ≈ 0.10. The Psychopath state has low overall probability (~5%) but disproportionate accident impact.
variables.quantitative_notes: Risk attitude is a latent trait in insurance modeling. The four-level discretization spans from clinical psychopathy (thrill-seeking, no consequence evaluation) to pathological caution. In actuarial practice, proxy measures include speeding violations and prior claim history, both captured elsewhere in this network.

variables.name: VehicleYear
variables.label: Vehicle model year
variables.description: Vehicle recency; proxy for safety technology availability.
variables.mechanism: Root node. VehicleYear is the temporal technology proxy: Current vehicles have substantially higher probability of having Antilock brakes, Airbags, and AntiTheft systems than older vehicles. It also contributes to CarValue (depreciation means older vehicles are worth less). VehicleYear is the key root node connecting model-year to three downstream safety and value nodes.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(Antilock=True | VehicleYear=Current) ≈ 0.85; P(Antilock=True | VehicleYear=older) ≈ 0.40. P(Airbag=True | VehicleYear=Current, MakeModel=Economy) ≈ 0.75; P(Airbag=True | VehicleYear=older, MakeModel=Economy) ≈ 0.25.
variables.quantitative_notes: ABS became mandatory in the US for new passenger cars in 2013. Airbags were mandatory from 1998. AntiTheft (immobilizers) became prevalent post-2000. VehicleYear=Current therefore serves as a composite mandatory-safety-equipment flag in the ALARM-era model.

variables.name: ThisCarDam
variables.label: Damage to insured car
variables.description: Physical damage severity to the insured vehicle.
variables.mechanism: ThisCarDam is jointly determined by Accident severity (more severe accident → more damage) and RuggedAuto (structural protection moderates damage given accident severity). The interaction is multiplicative: Accident=Severe + RuggedAuto=EggShell → near-certain Severe damage; Accident=Mild + RuggedAuto=Tank → likely None or Mild. ThisCarDam directly drives ThisCarCost.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(ThisCarDam=Severe | Accident=Severe, RuggedAuto=EggShell) ≈ 0.90; P(ThisCarDam=Severe | Accident=Severe, RuggedAuto=Tank) ≈ 0.35; P(ThisCarDam=None | Accident=None) = 1.
variables.quantitative_notes: The RuggedAuto moderating effect is the primary structural reason why the same accident severity produces different insurance claims across vehicle classes. SUVs and trucks (Tank) often sustain less structural damage in collisions but can cause more damage to other vehicles — an asymmetry relevant to third-party liability.

variables.name: RuggedAuto
variables.label: Vehicle structural ruggedness
variables.description: Structural crashworthiness category; moderates accident-to-damage translation.
variables.mechanism: RuggedAuto is determined by MakeModel: SportsCar/Economy → EggShell (lightweight, poor crash structure); FamilySedan → Football (average); Luxury/SuperLuxury → Tank (high-strength steel, crumple zones). RuggedAuto moderates ThisCarDam and jointly determines Cushioning (with Airbag). It is the primary vehicle-side damage moderation node.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(RuggedAuto=Tank | MakeModel=SuperLuxury) ≈ 0.75; P(RuggedAuto=EggShell | MakeModel=SportsCar) ≈ 0.65; P(RuggedAuto=Football | MakeModel=FamilySedan) ≈ 0.70.
variables.quantitative_notes: NHTSA crash test ratings map broadly: 5-star vehicles → Tank; 3-star → Football; 1-2 star or unrated → EggShell. The RuggedAuto node captures the interaction between vehicle mass and structural engineering, both of which increase systematically from Economy through SuperLuxury.

variables.name: Accident
variables.label: Accident severity
variables.description: Overall accident severity; the central loss event node.
variables.mechanism: Accident is the central hub of the loss sub-network. It is determined by DrivQuality (proximate behavioural cause), Mileage (exposure), Antilock (active safety mitigation), and OtherCar (multi-vehicle amplification of severity). It simultaneously drives ThisCarDam (own vehicle), OtherCarCost (third-party), and MedCost (injuries). Accident is the highest-fanout outcome node in the network.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(Accident=Severe | DrivQuality=Poor, Mileage=Domino, Antilock=False, OtherCar=True) ≈ 0.35; P(Accident=None | DrivQuality=Excellent, Mileage=FiveThou, Antilock=True, OtherCar=False) ≈ 0.75. Antilock=True reduces P(Severe) by approximately 10–15 percentage points.
variables.quantitative_notes: Accident is the key d-separation node between the driver sub-network and all cost nodes. Conditioning on Accident renders ThisCarDam, OtherCarCost, and MedCost independent of DrivQuality, Mileage, Antilock, and OtherCar. This makes Accident the most important variable for claim triage: knowing accident severity allows cost estimation without driver profile data.

variables.name: MakeModel
variables.label: Car make/model class
variables.description: Vehicle class; the primary vehicle-side root determining all vehicle attributes.
variables.mechanism: MakeModel is determined by SocioEcon. It is the most connected vehicle node: it determines RuggedAuto (crash structure), CarValue (market price), Antilock availability, Airbag availability, and indirectly AntiTheft. MakeModel is the key common cause for all vehicle attribute nodes, making it a critical fork in the vehicle sub-network.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(CarValue=FiftyThou or Million | MakeModel=SuperLuxury) ≈ 0.80; P(Airbag=True | MakeModel=Luxury, VehicleYear=Current) ≈ 0.99; P(Antilock=True | MakeModel=Economy, VehicleYear=older) ≈ 0.25.
variables.quantitative_notes: MakeModel is the central fork node in the vehicle sub-network: all four vehicle attribute children (RuggedAuto, CarValue, Antilock, Airbag) are conditionally independent of SocioEcon given MakeModel. This makes MakeModel the key variable for vehicle-specific actuarial rating: knowing MakeModel is as informative as knowing SocioEcon for vehicle-related risks.

variables.name: DrivQuality
variables.label: Driving quality
variables.description: Synthesized driving performance; the proximate cause of accident risk.
variables.mechanism: DrivQuality integrates DrivingSkill (technical competency) and RiskAversion (behavioural disposition). The interaction is approximately multiplicative: Expert skill + Cautious attitude → Excellent; SubStandard skill + Psychopath attitude → Poor (certain). A skilled but reckless driver (Expert + Adventurous) tends toward Normal, not Excellent. DrivQuality is the direct proximate cause of Accident severity, rendering Accident conditionally independent of DrivingSkill and RiskAversion given DrivQuality.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(DrivQuality=Excellent | DrivingSkill=Expert, RiskAversion=Cautious) ≈ 0.75; P(DrivQuality=Poor | DrivingSkill=SubStandard, RiskAversion=Psychopath) ≈ 0.90; P(DrivQuality=Normal | DrivingSkill=Normal, RiskAversion=Normal) ≈ 0.65.
variables.quantitative_notes: DrivQuality is the information bottleneck between the driver profile sub-network and the accident/cost sub-network. Given DrivQuality, the accident risk is independent of all upstream driver profile variables (Age, SocioEcon, GoodStudent, DrivHist, SeniorTrain). This makes it the most important single variable for risk classification.

variables.name: Mileage
variables.label: Annual mileage bucket
variables.description: Annual miles driven; pure exposure multiplier on accident risk.
variables.mechanism: Mileage is influenced by RiskAversion (risk-seeking drivers drive more). It functions as an exposure variable: holding DrivQuality constant, higher mileage increases accident probability proportionally to kilometres at risk. Domino represents extreme mileage (commercial or rideshare level, ~100k+ miles/year). Mileage also affects OtherCar probability (more driving in dense areas).
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(Mileage=Domino | RiskAversion=Psychopath) ≈ 0.25; P(Mileage=FiveThou | RiskAversion=Cautious) ≈ 0.45. Mileage and DrivQuality have independent additive effects on P(Accident=Severe).
variables.quantitative_notes: Insurance usage-based telematics: each additional 10,000 annual miles raises accident probability by approximately 15–25% independent of driving quality. The Domino level (extreme mileage) models commercial drivers, who despite often having Expert skill have high Accident rates purely from exposure. This exposure-skill independence is a key insight: Domino + Excellent DrivQuality still produces higher Accident probability than FiveThou + Poor DrivQuality.

variables.name: Antilock
variables.label: Antilock braking system (ABS)
variables.description: ABS presence; active safety system reducing accident severity.
variables.mechanism: Antilock is determined by MakeModel (standard on Luxury/SuperLuxury) and VehicleYear (Current vehicles). When True, ABS directly reduces P(Accident=Severe or Moderate) by maintaining steering control during hard braking. It is conditionally independent of driver profile nodes given MakeModel and VehicleYear.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(Antilock=True | MakeModel=Luxury, VehicleYear=Current) ≈ 0.99; P(Antilock=True | MakeModel=Economy, VehicleYear=older) ≈ 0.25. ABS reduces P(Accident=Severe) by approximately 0.10–0.15.
variables.quantitative_notes: NHTSA studies: ABS reduces fatal crash involvement by ~6% for cars, ~35% for motorcycles. In the Insurance BN, Antilock is one of two active safety features (with Airbag) that directly reduce adverse outcomes. Antilock reduces accident severity; Airbag reduces injury given accident. These operate at different points in the causal chain.

variables.name: DrivingSkill
variables.label: Driver skill level
variables.description: Technical driving competency; the skill component of driving quality.
variables.mechanism: DrivingSkill is determined by three inputs: Age (inexperience in Adolescents, decline in Seniors), SeniorTrain (completed training improves Senior skill), and DrivHist (more prior incidents → lower skill rating). DrivingSkill feeds DrivQuality as the technical component, interacting with RiskAversion. Given DrivQuality, DrivingSkill is conditionally independent of Accident.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(DrivingSkill=Expert | Age=Adult, DrivHist=Zero, SeniorTrain=False) ≈ 0.25; P(DrivingSkill=SubStandard | Age=Adolescent, DrivHist=Many) ≈ 0.80; P(DrivingSkill=Normal | Age=Senior, SeniorTrain=True) ≈ 0.55.
variables.quantitative_notes: Driving skill and risk aversion are approximately orthogonal in the Insurance model — both independently affect DrivQuality. This creates four meaningful driver archetypes: Skilled+Cautious (Excellent DrivQuality), Skilled+Reckless (Normal), Unskilled+Cautious (Normal-Poor), Unskilled+Reckless (Poor-certain). The SeniorTrain intervention can shift seniors from SubStandard toward Normal, reducing accident risk.

variables.name: SeniorTrain
variables.label: Senior driver training
variables.description: Completion of senior driver refresher program; Age-conditional intervention.
variables.mechanism: SeniorTrain is available only to Senior-age drivers (Age=Senior prerequisite). When True, it improves DrivingSkill. It is a targeted intervention node: its effect is zero for non-Seniors (P(SeniorTrain=True | Age=Adolescent or Adult) ≈ 0). This makes SeniorTrain a key node for policy interventions targeting the Senior segment.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(SeniorTrain=True | Age=Senior) ≈ 0.30; P(SeniorTrain=True | Age=Adolescent) ≈ 0.001; P(SeniorTrain=True | Age=Adult) ≈ 0.005. Effect: P(DrivingSkill=Normal | Age=Senior, SeniorTrain=True) ≈ 0.55 vs. 0.35 without training.
variables.quantitative_notes: AARP SmartDriver program data: completion reduces crash risk by ~8% for senior drivers. The Insurance BN captures this as a direct improvement in DrivingSkill, which then propagates to DrivQuality and Accident. SeniorTrain is the only modeled intervention node — the only node where policy (insurance discount, mandatory training) can directly shift outcomes.

variables.name: ThisCarCost
variables.label: Insured car claim cost
variables.description: Total financial cost for the insured vehicle (repair or total loss).
variables.mechanism: ThisCarCost is determined by two independent pathways: (1) damage pathway: ThisCarDam × CarValue (damage severity × replacement cost basis); (2) theft pathway: Theft × CarValue (total loss value). Both pathways interact through CarValue, making CarValue the key moderating variable for all this-car financial outcomes. ThisCarCost feeds PropCost.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(ThisCarCost=Million | ThisCarDam=Severe, CarValue=Million) ≈ 0.85; P(ThisCarCost=Thousand | Theft=False, ThisCarDam=None) = 1; P(ThisCarCost=HundredThou | Theft=True, CarValue=FiftyThou) ≈ 0.70.
variables.quantitative_notes: The two-pathway structure of ThisCarCost (damage + theft) means it can be HIGH even when Accident=None (theft-only claim). This is a critical diagnostic pattern: high ThisCarCost with Accident=None is pathognomonic for Theft=True. The correlation between MakeModel and CarValue creates a systematic pattern where Luxury vehicle owners face both higher potential costs and higher theft risk.

variables.name: Theft
variables.label: Vehicle theft
variables.description: Whether the insured vehicle was stolen.
variables.mechanism: Theft probability is determined by three factors: CarValue (more valuable cars more targeted), HomeBase (City highest crime; Secure lowest), and AntiTheft (deterrence reduces probability). These combine as: attractive target (CarValue) × access opportunity (HomeBase) × deterrence (AntiTheft). Theft feeds ThisCarCost as a total-loss pathway independent of the accident pathway.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(Theft=True | CarValue=Million, HomeBase=City, AntiTheft=False) ≈ 0.25; P(Theft=True | CarValue=FiveThou, HomeBase=Secure, AntiTheft=True) ≈ 0.02; P(Theft=True | CarValue=FiftyThou, HomeBase=City, AntiTheft=False) ≈ 0.15.
variables.quantitative_notes: NICB data: vehicles valued > $50K are stolen at 3–5× the rate of vehicles < $10K. Urban areas have 2–4× higher theft rates than suburban/rural areas. Immobilizers and GPS tracking (AntiTheft) reduce theft by 40–60%. The Theft node creates an important v-structure with AntiTheft and CarValue: given Theft status, AntiTheft and CarValue become dependent (explaining-away — if Theft=True and AntiTheft=True, CarValue=high is more likely).

variables.name: CarValue
variables.label: Insured car value
variables.description: Market value of the insured vehicle; the financial scale parameter for all property costs.
variables.mechanism: CarValue is determined by MakeModel (primary value driver: SuperLuxury → Million; Economy → FiveThou) and VehicleYear (Current → higher value due to no depreciation). CarValue is a common cause of two important downstream nodes: Theft (attractive target) and ThisCarCost (replacement cost ceiling). It is the financial scale moderator for all property-related costs.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(CarValue=Million | MakeModel=SuperLuxury, VehicleYear=Current) ≈ 0.70; P(CarValue=FiveThou | MakeModel=Economy, VehicleYear=older) ≈ 0.65; P(CarValue=FiftyThou | MakeModel=Luxury, VehicleYear=older) ≈ 0.40.
variables.quantitative_notes: CarValue is a fork with two children (Theft and ThisCarCost), creating a confounding path: Theft and ThisCarCost are marginally correlated (both driven by high CarValue) but are conditionally independent given CarValue. This is the canonical fork structure in the Insurance network's financial sub-tree. Actuarially, separating theft risk premium from collision cost premium requires controlling for CarValue.

variables.name: HomeBase
variables.label: Home neighbourhood type
variables.description: Residential neighbourhood type; ambient risk environment.
variables.mechanism: HomeBase is determined by SocioEcon (Wealthy → Secure; Prole → City primarily). It influences two downstream nodes: Theft (City has highest crime density) and OtherCar (City traffic density increases multi-vehicle collision probability). HomeBase is the bridge node between socio-economic status and environmental risk.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(HomeBase=City | SocioEcon=Prole) ≈ 0.50; P(HomeBase=Secure | SocioEcon=Wealthy) ≈ 0.55; P(HomeBase=Rural | SocioEcon=Middle) ≈ 0.25.
variables.quantitative_notes: Urban density creates two distinct risk pathways: (1) theft risk via criminal opportunity and (2) multi-vehicle accident risk via traffic congestion. These are independent effects of HomeBase, making City the highest-risk neighbourhood level on both dimensions. Conditioning on HomeBase blocks the SocioEcon→Theft and SocioEcon→OtherCar paths, making HomeBase the key mediator for neighbourhood-based risk assessment.

variables.name: AntiTheft
variables.label: Anti-theft system
variables.description: Anti-theft device; primary deterrent reducing theft probability.
variables.mechanism: AntiTheft presence is determined by MakeModel (standard on Luxury/SuperLuxury) and VehicleYear (Current vehicles more likely equipped). AntiTheft has a single downstream effect: directly reducing Theft probability. It has no effect on accident severity, driving quality, or any cost node other than through Theft.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(AntiTheft=True | MakeModel=SuperLuxury, VehicleYear=Current) ≈ 0.95; P(AntiTheft=True | MakeModel=Economy, VehicleYear=older) ≈ 0.15.
variables.quantitative_notes: AntiTheft and CarValue both influence Theft, creating a v-structure: Theft ← AntiTheft → ... and Theft ← CarValue → .... Conditioning on Theft activates explaining-away between AntiTheft and CarValue. This is actuarially important: if a high-value car is stolen despite having AntiTheft=True, that is a more surprising event (and may trigger fraud investigation) than if AntiTheft=False.

variables.name: PropCost
variables.label: Proportional cost comparison
variables.description: Relative cost summary comparing insured-car to other-car costs.
variables.mechanism: PropCost aggregates ThisCarCost and OtherCarCost into a comparative cost ratio used for policy pricing and claim reserve estimation. It is a terminal aggregation leaf — the highest-level cost summary node in the network with no downstream effects.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: PropCost tracks the maximum of ThisCarCost and OtherCarCost in most parameterizations: P(PropCost=Million | ThisCarCost=Million) ≈ 0.90 regardless of OtherCarCost.
variables.quantitative_notes: PropCost is one of four terminal cost leaves (with ThisCarCost, ILiCost, and implicitly MedCost). In the original Insurance BN, PropCost represents the insurer's total property liability and is the primary output for premium calculation. Given both parent costs, PropCost is conditionally independent of all other nodes — the classic leaf-node conditional independence property.

variables.name: OtherCarCost
variables.label: Other car claim cost
variables.description: Third-party vehicle cost; liability cost for the other vehicle.
variables.mechanism: OtherCarCost is determined by Accident severity and OtherCar (prerequisite: if OtherCar=False, OtherCarCost=Thousand with near-certainty). Severe multi-vehicle accidents with an involved third party (OtherCar=True) produce the highest OtherCarCost. OtherCarCost feeds PropCost.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(OtherCarCost=Thousand | OtherCar=False) ≈ 0.97; P(OtherCarCost=HundredThou | Accident=Severe, OtherCar=True) ≈ 0.35; P(OtherCarCost=Million | Accident=Severe, OtherCar=True) ≈ 0.15.
variables.quantitative_notes: Third-party property damage is the second-largest cost category in auto insurance after bodily injury. The OtherCar=True prerequisite creates a zero-inflated cost distribution: most policies have OtherCar=False (single-vehicle incidents), making OtherCarCost=Thousand the modal outcome. The OtherCar + Accident interaction produces the full distribution.

variables.name: OtherCar
variables.label: Other vehicle involved
variables.description: Whether a second vehicle participates in the incident.
variables.mechanism: OtherCar is influenced by HomeBase (City traffic density increases multi-vehicle collision probability) and Mileage (more driving exposure increases encounter probability). OtherCar=True both amplifies Accident severity (multi-vehicle crashes are more severe) and is the prerequisite for OtherCarCost. This creates a v-structure at Accident (DrivQuality → Accident ← OtherCar) that is important for explaining-away inference.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(OtherCar=True | HomeBase=City, Mileage=Domino) ≈ 0.55; P(OtherCar=True | HomeBase=Rural, Mileage=FiveThou) ≈ 0.10.
variables.quantitative_notes: Multi-vehicle crashes account for ~55% of fatal crashes in urban areas vs. ~30% in rural areas (NHTSA). The OtherCar node is the bridge between the environment sub-network (HomeBase) and the accident severity pathway. Conditioning on OtherCar=True and Accident=Severe creates explaining-away between DrivQuality and OtherCar: if the accident was severe and involved another car, it was less likely due to poor driving alone.

variables.name: MedCost
variables.label: Medical treatment cost
variables.description: Medical cost of accident-related injuries.
variables.mechanism: MedCost is jointly determined by Accident severity (more severe accident → more injuries) and Cushioning quality (Poor cushioning amplifies injury given accident). These interact multiplicatively: Severe accident + Poor cushioning → near-certain HundredThou/Million costs; Mild accident + Excellent cushioning → Thousand. MedCost feeds ILiCost.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(MedCost=Million | Accident=Severe, Cushioning=Poor) ≈ 0.40; P(MedCost=HundredThou | Accident=Severe, Cushioning=Excellent) ≈ 0.25; P(MedCost=Thousand | Accident=None) = 1.
variables.quantitative_notes: Medical/bodily injury costs are the largest single category in auto insurance claims (~40% of total losses). The Cushioning moderating effect captures the well-documented finding that airbags reduce injury severity by ~30% in frontal collisions. MedCost and ThisCarCost are conditionally independent given Accident — a key property for claims triage: vehicle damage and injury costs provide independent information about accident severity when accident severity itself is not directly observed.

variables.name: Cushioning
variables.label: Occupant cushioning quality
variables.description: Integrated occupant protection quality; modulates injury severity given accident.
variables.mechanism: Cushioning is determined by Airbag (primary active protection component) and RuggedAuto (structural passive protection). The two inputs interact: Airbag=True + RuggedAuto=Tank → almost certainly Excellent; Airbag=False + RuggedAuto=EggShell → almost certainly Poor. Cushioning then moderates how Accident severity translates into MedCost.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(Cushioning=Excellent | Airbag=True, RuggedAuto=Tank) ≈ 0.85; P(Cushioning=Poor | Airbag=False, RuggedAuto=EggShell) ≈ 0.80; P(Cushioning=Good | Airbag=True, RuggedAuto=Football) ≈ 0.60.
variables.quantitative_notes: Cushioning is the d-separation node between the vehicle safety sub-network (Airbag, RuggedAuto) and medical cost outcomes. Given Cushioning, MedCost is conditionally independent of Airbag, RuggedAuto, MakeModel, and VehicleYear. This means knowing Cushioning quality allows accurate injury cost prediction without needing vehicle specification data — an important simplification for real-time claim estimation.

variables.name: Airbag
variables.label: Airbag present
variables.description: Airbag availability; primary active occupant protection system.
variables.mechanism: Airbag is determined by MakeModel (standard on Luxury/SuperLuxury; rare on older Economy) and VehicleYear (Current vehicles standard-equipped post-1998 mandate). Airbag is the dominant input to Cushioning quality; its presence reduces MedCost through improved Cushioning. Given MakeModel and VehicleYear, Airbag is conditionally independent of all driver profile nodes.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(Airbag=True | MakeModel=Luxury, VehicleYear=Current) ≈ 0.99; P(Airbag=True | MakeModel=Economy, VehicleYear=Current) ≈ 0.75; P(Airbag=True | MakeModel=Economy, VehicleYear=older) ≈ 0.25.
variables.quantitative_notes: NHTSA: frontal airbags reduce driver fatality risk by 29% in direct frontal crashes. Airbag and Antilock operate at different causal stages: Antilock reduces accident probability; Airbag reduces injury given accident. They are not causally related — their effects are independent — but both are determined by the same parents (MakeModel, VehicleYear), making them marginally correlated (via common cause) but conditionally independent given those parents.

variables.name: ILiCost
variables.label: Injury / liability cost
variables.description: Total injury and legal liability cost; terminal liability cost leaf.
variables.mechanism: ILiCost aggregates MedCost (direct injury costs) into a total injury-and-liability bucket that incorporates third-party bodily injury liability, legal defence costs, and pain-and-suffering settlements. It is a terminal leaf node with no downstream effects in the model.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: ILiCost tracks MedCost closely but is systematically higher due to liability multipliers: P(ILiCost=Million | MedCost=HundredThou) ≈ 0.35 (litigation risk); P(ILiCost=Thousand | MedCost=Thousand) ≈ 0.90.
variables.quantitative_notes: Bodily injury liability is the most variable cost component in auto insurance: small injuries can become large settlements via litigation. ILiCost > MedCost by the liability multiplier captures this legal risk. In the Insurance BN, ILiCost is one of two terminal cost summary leaves (with PropCost), representing the insurer's total bodily-injury liability exposure. Insurers use ILiCost predictions to set policy limits and reserve amounts.

variables.name: DrivHist
variables.label: Prior driving incidents
variables.description: Bucketed count of prior at-fault accidents or moving violations.
variables.mechanism: Root node with no modeled parents. DrivHist is a historical record that directly informs DrivingSkill: Many incidents → SubStandard skill much more probable. It is also the primary observable actuarial risk indicator, as it is the most reliable predictor of future claims. DrivHist is causally upstream of DrivingSkill only — it does not directly affect RiskAversion or any vehicle node.
variables.cpt_shape_hints: P(DrivingSkill=SubStandard | DrivHist=Many) ≈ 0.65; P(DrivingSkill=Expert | DrivHist=Zero, Age=Adult) ≈ 0.30; P(DrivingSkill=Normal | DrivHist=One, Age=Adult) ≈ 0.60.
variables.quantitative_notes: Insurance industry: the single strongest predictor of future claims is prior claims history. A driver with 2+ prior at-fault accidents (DrivHist=Many) has 3–4× the expected future claim frequency of a zero-history driver. DrivHist is the key observable root node for actuarial experience rating. Importantly, it is causally upstream of skill (not of risk aversion), meaning that incident history informs us about competency rather than attitude — a distinction that matters for distinguishing unlucky skilled drivers from genuinely unskilled ones.
